source.title: On the Generalization Benefit of Noise in Stochastic Gradient Descent
source.authors: Samuel L. Smith; Erich Elsen; Soham De

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how batch size and gradient noise affect training loss and test generalization. It does not test whether large networks reach zero or near-zero training classification error, nor any of V1–V6 as stated.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training losses, not training classification errors. Those loss results do not establish whether the claim's predicted classification-error behavior occurs. Its cited findings from other studies are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study's own comparison of Wide-ResNet training with and without batch normalization bears on V6: Appendix C.2 explicitly reports a significantly smaller critical learning rate without batch normalization. The extracted training-loss rows do not capture this comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that stochastic gradient noise can improve test generalization even with tuned learning rates and equal update counts. They also find evidence that a large initial training temperature benefits generalization in most tested models, while restricting their conclusions to the schedules and architectures studied.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines batch-size and gradient-noise effects on generalization, rather than the claim's training classification error or any listed version.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with batch size, normalization, architecture, dataset, and epoch budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Under fixed update budgets, larger batches generally attain smaller final training losses, while very large batches can have worse test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stochastic gradient noise can improve generalization despite higher final training loss under the tested schedules.

record.problems: The paper's reported training losses do not measure classification error, and the text does not report whether classification error reaches zero or near zero.
record.rows_left_out: Other training-loss results under constant-step budgets and training-loss curves across epoch budgets are omitted because they are additional loss measurements and do not establish classification error. See Tables 3 and 5 and Figures 1–3, 5–10.

untested.parts: Training classification error, including random or corrupted labels and dependence on model size, stopping time, and regularization.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious local minima, and additional student neurons.
Depth-related degradation and matched comparisons of plain networks with identity shortcuts.
Comparative effects of activation-matched, Gaussian, and orthogonal initializations on training speed and trainable depth; using Regularized SkipInit alone does not test these effects.
Recovery above the initial linearized stability limit, transient loss and curvature dynamics, and prolonged tracking of the stability threshold.
A demonstrated comparison of accuracy-gain speed, the originally specified architectures, and Fixup's speed and stability relative to normalization.

missing.what: Record the comparison showing significantly lower critical learning rates without batch normalization. With normalization, vanilla SGD's optimal learning rate levels off around batch size 512; without normalization, its performance begins degrading around batch size 8. These batch-size thresholds contextualize the comparison but are not numerical measurements of the critical learning rate. The unnormalized model uses Regularized SkipInit.
missing.locator: Section 5, Figure 1(c); Appendix C.2, Figure 6(c) and accompanying discussion.

record.verdict_notes: The record overlooks an empirical normalization comparison relevant to V6. Its training-loss values are correctly transcribed, but they do not directly report training classification error. Discussion of the quadratic stability threshold does not establish V5's recovery or sharpness dynamics. Reported Wide-ResNet means use the best 12 of 15 runs, so failed or outlier runs are excluded.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and the stated model-size and training-duration conditions.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth-related training error and the effects of identity shortcuts.
Initialization effects on training speed and trainable depth.
Training behavior above the stability limit and sharpness dynamics.
Whether batch normalization speeds accuracy gains or increases learning-rate tolerance, and whether Fixup matches its training speed and stability.

relationships.condition: 16-4 Wide-ResNet on CIFAR-10, 200 epochs; ghost batch normalization versus no normalization with Regularized SkipInit.
relationships.reason: Based on text rather than existing rows: Appendix C.2 reports a significantly smaller critical learning rate without batch normalization, supporting greater learning-rate tolerance with normalization; the comparison also changes initialization.
relationships.display_finding: The unnormalized Regularized SkipInit recipe had a significantly smaller critical learning rate, although initialization also differed.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
